body_html:
How to say your age in Spanish is one of the first things learners need, and one of the first mistakes they make. English uses “to be”: “I am 30”. Spanish uses tener, to have: Tengo 30 años, literally “I have 30 years”. Saying Soy 30 is a direct translation that Spanish speakers will understand, but it sounds clearly foreign. Here’s everything you need, from the basic phrase to polite ways of asking and the spelling trap that can turn your age into something embarrassing.

Key takeaways
  • Age uses tener: Tengo 25 años.
  • Ask with ¿Cuántos años tienes? (or tiene with usted).
  • Birthdays use cumplir: Mañana cumplo 40.
  • Always write años with the ñ.
{{toc}}

How to say your age in Spanish: the basic phrase

EnglishSpanish
I’m 30.Tengo 30 años.
She’s 8.Tiene 8 años.
We’re both 40.Los dos tenemos 40 años.
My baby is 6 months old.Mi bebé tiene 6 meses.
How old are you?¿Cuántos años tienes?

In conversation you can drop años: —¿Cuántos tienes? —Treinta. The RAE dictionary lists this use of tener to express age.

Asking someone’s age

  • ¿Cuántos años tienes? How old are you? (informal)
  • ¿Cuántos años tiene usted? (formal)
  • ¿Qué edad tiene? What age is he/she? (neutral, slightly formal)
  • ¿Cuántos años tiene tu hijo? How old is your son?

As in English, asking adults their age can feel personal, especially with older people. With children, it is a common friendly question.

Birthdays: cumplir años

  • Hoy cumplo 35. I turn 35 today.
  • ¿Cuándo cumples años? When is your birthday?
  • Voy a cumplir 50 en mayo. I’ll be 50 in May.
  • ¡Que cumplas muchos más! Many happy returns!

For birthday messages, see {{link:birthday-wishes-in-spanish|birthday wishes in Spanish}}.

{{image:2}}

Approximate and descriptive ages

  • Tiene unos 40 años. He’s about 40.
  • Tengo treinta y pocos. I’m in my early thirties.
  • Tiene cuarenta y tantos. She’s in her forties (forty-something).
  • Ronda los sesenta. He’s around sixty.
  • Está en los veinte. She’s in her twenties.
  • un hombre de 30 años a 30-year-old man

Older, younger and age words

  • Mi hermano mayor / menor. My older / younger brother.
  • Soy dos años mayor que ella. I’m two years older than her.
  • una persona mayor an elderly person (polite; better than viejo)
  • la tercera edad old age, senior citizens
  • ser mayor de edad / menor de edad to be an adult / a minor
{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

The año trap

Spelling matters here more than anywhere: años means years, but anos without the ñ is the plural of a word for a part of the body. Writing Tengo 30 anos in a message is a famous slip. On a phone, long-press the n to get ñ. More in {{link:spanish-accent-marks|Spanish accent marks}} and {{link:embarrassing-spanish-mistakes|embarrassing Spanish mistakes}}.

Why this happens

English describes age as a state you are in, while Spanish treats it as something you have accumulated, like experience. The same logic explains tengo hambre, tengo frío and tengo miedo: physical states and conditions that English expresses with “be”. I group these in {{link:literal-translation-mistakes-spanish|literal translation mistakes in Spanish}}. Learning them together as a family is the fastest way to stop translating “to be”.

Real conversation

  • A: ¡Qué guapa tu hija! ¿Cuántos años tiene? (Your daughter is lovely! How old is she?)
  • B: Tiene cinco, pero el mes que viene cumple seis. (She’s five, but she turns six next month.)
  • A: ¿Y tu hijo? (And your son?)
  • B: Es dos años mayor. Tiene ocho. (He’s two years older. He’s eight.)

Ages in writing: numbers or words?

In everyday messages, numbers are fine: Tengo 34 años. In formal or literary writing, Spanish style guides prefer words for ages under one hundred: Tenía treinta y cuatro años cuando se mudó a Lima. Remember that numbers from 16 to 29 are written as one word (dieciséis, veintidós, veintinueve), while from 31 onwards they use y (treinta y uno, cuarenta y cinco). And when you write about decades, use plural words without an apostrophe: los años noventa (the nineties), never los 90’s.

Try it yourself

  1. I’m 27. (Tengo 27 años.)
  2. How old is your mother? (¿Cuántos años tiene tu madre?)
  3. I turn 30 on Saturday. (El sábado cumplo 30.)
  4. He’s in his fifties. (Tiene cincuenta y tantos.)
  5. My sister is three years younger than me. (Mi hermana es tres años menor que yo.)

All mistake types in {{link:common-spanish-mistakes|my guide to common Spanish mistakes}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

In Spanish you have your age: tengo, tienes, tiene. You turn a new age with cumplir. And you always write años with its ñ. Three small rules, and one of the most common beginner mistakes is gone for good.

faq.q: How do you say your age in Spanish?
faq.a: Use tener: Tengo 30 años (I’m 30). Spanish does not use ser or estar for age.

faq.q: How do you ask “How old are you?” in Spanish?
faq.a: ¿Cuántos años tienes? (informal) or ¿Cuántos años tiene usted? (formal).

faq.q: How do you say “I’m turning 40” in Spanish?
faq.a: Voy a cumplir 40, or Cumplo 40 on the day itself.

questions.explain: The natural question uses cuántos años.
